P1.evidence: The strongest open in the batch. The rep recapped the prior call in full and accurately before doing anything else — 'before I go anywhere, I just want to make sure I haven't missed anything. So let me just, like, make a summary of what we did. So you're 39, around 105 kilos... You're suffering from disc compression, some unstable knee problem, and tight hips... you're running your own company... for the past two years, your blood pressure has been elevated' — and checked it back: 'That's still the right target for you.' The four-part frame was not re-set, which is defensible on a continuation call but still incomplete. The open question ran as a consequence-shaped one: 'if nothing changed over the next few years, like, what concerns you the most?'

P2.evidence: Baseline belongs to the 05/26 call and is scored there. The recap here was accurate and complete on every fact previously gathered, so nothing is lost by dropping the phase from this denominator.

P3.evidence: Surface goals were established on the prior call, so P3a and P3b drop out. The can't-do-it question ran and landed on the best material of the call — the prospect volunteered that he has not run since the knee injury and remembers how fast he was, and the rep followed with 'Would you like to get back to it?' The future-self question ran well too: 'when you think about it, actually, what does that version of Marian feel like?', producing 'I will be too cool', which the rep then reused as the close language. The impact-on-others and legacy layers were again supplied by the rep rather than elicited — 'you're doing it not only for yourself, but for your family' — and the reflect-back was a reframe rather than a mirror: 'you're an entrepreneur, like you run a business, you are successful... But with health, like even the great football players, basketball players, all need coaches.'

P4.evidence: The rep called back to the prior call rather than re-asking, which is right, and the prospect volunteered the pattern himself in unusually precise terms: 'I tried and I give up. And I tried and I give up and I like giving up. You know, it's not like giving up. It's like finding ways to give up.' The rep matched it with the Monday image — 'It will be like Monday, and Monday, and Monday. And this Monday never comes' — and later added the holiday relapse. P4f ran cleanly in its own idiom: 'even the great football players, basketball players, all need coaches. Yeah, even though they could be doing themselves, but they need this extra support.' The gap-naming was collaborative rather than elicited, so those checks are partial.

P5.evidence: The only properly executed consequence question in the batch: 'when things will stay the same, like, if nothing changed over the next few years, like, what concerns you the most?' — and the rep built on the answer with the compensation argument ('when you have an injury... your body is going to overcompensate in other areas... your body actually changes in the wrong way'). The settle test appeared only as a statement — 'Because if you don't change anything, you know how it can go' — rather than a question, and the 'why not' never ran. The line in the sand was replaced with a permission ask, which is a strong variant but not the scripted move: 'do I have your permission to hold you accountable to all the things that you said that are important to you?'

P6.evidence: Textbook, and the only complete P6 in the batch. The belief check ran in full — 'If you had the right training, simple nutrition, and real accountability from Trevor, all built around your life... Do you agree that you would get to your 90 kilo, you would even start running and play with your daughters?' — and when the answer came back soft ('That would be nice') the rep refused to accept it: 'That would be nice? Or are you going to do it?' The all-in question ran essentially verbatim: 'If you had a, like a right structure, the right coach, and the right accountability, which is like crucial part over here, is there any reason you wouldn't go all on this?' And a clear yes was obtained and hardened before any number: 'Are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work to become the too cool version of Marian?' / '100%? You need to be 100% on this.' / 'I am 100%.'

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and a handshake obtained, and the rep laid out the correct order — 'We're going to go through the payment, and then I'm going to onboard you and book you a call with Trevor' — but payment was refused pending due diligence, and the fallback $100 deposit was refused too. Because step one never completed, the Trevor booking, the agreement email and signature, and the welcome-email and community walkthrough were all unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: '9K is a lot of money, to be honest' at 00:28:15. The isolate ran properly and twice — 'before we talk about numbers and money, do you actually feel that you can get to your goals with Trevor, and you're 100% sure on this? Is there anything else apart from money that could be stopping you?' — and produced a clean 'It's nothing else that can stop me.' The break-it-up move ran close to script: 'most of the guys pay upfront, but if there's a will, there is a way, we could split it up.' Everything after that did not run: no 'you're not in a should-I place, you're in a how place', no permission question for an open financial conversation, and none of the six financial-picture questions — cash on hand, monthly surplus, number of cards, available credit, used versus available, or investments. Instead of building the picture the rep downshifted the tier and then quoted financed instalments totalling more than the list price.

The prospect deferred the decision to the next day pending checks. Two OA-adjacent moves ran — 'So, so tell me, like, what's, what's coming up?' and 'are you looking for a reason to not to do it or just to be on the site?' — and the rep did secure a conditional commitment: 'if I would send you this information today or tomorrow and everything checks out and it's going to be fine, you ready to move forward?' Not run: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?', and 'that man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?', all of which had been set up perfectly by the prospect's own Monday-never-comes admission.

Worth recording because the play ran against a trigger that was not there. The prospect was not expressing fear or doubt about the outcome — he was stating a standard commercial verification process he applies to any vendor: 'I need to check what I used to check also in Denmark when I pay to a company.' The rep applied an OE-style reframe anyway — 'isn't that fear creeping in?' — which mislabels due diligence as an emotional obstacle. The prospect rejected the frame explicitly and it cost trust: 'I know the salespeople... here in Denmark, we don't do it in this way. We are, we give people time.'

Script gap — provider verification. The prospect asked for company details, information about Trevor, and references before releasing money: 'I think you have also some people who are satisfied or not satisfied with your job.' There is no scripted play and, on the evidence of this call, no collateral to send; the rep had to ask what was even wanted ('What kind of information would you need?') and then improvised a deposit. A one-page company and coach credential sheet would have closed this call.

Script gap — the clinical constellation, carried over from the prior call and restated by the rep himself in the opening recap. Disc compression, an unstable knee and two years of untreated elevated blood pressure were all named out loud, and there is no move in the playbook that pauses the sale for clearance. Instead the rep folded the medical facts into the pitch, treating them as one lifestyle problem with one solution and forecasting that the blood pressure would normalise.

notes: On the script this is the best call in the batch — a real consequence question, a complete commitment check, and a recap that made the prospect feel genuinely heard. Everything that went wrong went wrong after the yes: the money play stopped at 'we could split it up' instead of building a financial picture, so the rep improvised instalments that cost more than the list price against a prospect who believed he was paying six thousand monthly; and a routine verification request was answered with a fear reframe and a deposit ask, which is what actually lost the room. Coaching point: when a prospect who sells for a living asks to check you out, sending the information is the close.
